rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Give reasons for the following statements : (Any two)
(i) Benzaldehyde is less reactive than propanal in nucleophilic addition reactions.
(ii) Carboxylic acids do not give reactions of carbonyl group.
(iii) 4-nitrobenzoic acid is a stronger acid than benzoic acid.
rows.solution:
(i) Because the PHENYL GROUP relieves the carbonyl carbon of positive charge and crowds it.

Nucleophilic addition begins with attack on the carbonyl carbon, so it is faster the more POSITIVE and the more ACCESSIBLE that carbon is.

In benzaldehyde the ring is CONJUGATED with the carbonyl group, so the \(\pi\) system extends into it and the positive charge is delocalised over the ring — resonance structures can be drawn placing it at the ortho and para carbons. Propanal's ethyl group offers no such relief, releasing density only weakly by induction.

The flat ring is also bulkier than an ethyl group, so it hinders the nucleophile's approach as well.

(ii) Because the carboxyl carbon is stabilised by RESONANCE with the hydroxyl oxygen.

In a carboxylic acid the \(-\mathrm{OH}\) oxygen donates a lone pair into the carbonyl group, so the carbon carries far LESS positive charge than a plain carbonyl carbon does — in effect it loses its carbonyl character, and a nucleophile finds little to attack.

An aldehyde or ketone has no such donor beside it, only hydrogen or alkyl groups, which cannot supply a lone pair. So carboxylic acids give none of the characteristic additions: no bisulphite adduct, no cyanohydrin, no condensation with ammonia derivatives.

(iii) Because the NITRO GROUP stabilises the anion left behind.

Acid strength is decided by the stability of the carboxylate ion. The nitro group withdraws electron density both INDUCTIVELY and by RESONANCE, and from the PARA position its resonance reaches the carboxyl group directly, spreading the negative charge onto the nitro oxygens as well.

A more widely spread charge is a more stable anion, so the acid is stronger — \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) 3.44 against benzoic acid's 4.19.

rows.stem:
(i) Write the electronic configuration of \(d^4\) on the basis of crystal field splitting theory, if \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}} < \mathrm{P}\).
(ii) \(\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}}\) with square-planar structure is diamagnetic and \(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}\) with tetrahedral geometry is paramagnetic. Give reason to support the statement.
[Atomic number : Ni = 28]
(iii) Write the number of ions produced in the solution from the following complex :
\(\mathrm{[PtCl_2(NH_3)_4]Cl_2}\)
rows.solution:
(i) The configuration is \(t_{2g}^3\,e_g^1\).

An octahedral field splits the d orbitals into a lower set of three and an upper set of two, separated by \(\Delta_0\). Each electron chooses between promotion to the upper set, costing \(\Delta_0\), and pairing in the lower set, costing the pairing energy \(\mathrm{P}\).

With \(\Delta_0 < \mathrm{P}\) — a WEAK FIELD — promotion is the cheaper option, so the FOURTH electron goes upstairs rather than pairing. All four remain unpaired: a HIGH SPIN complex with \(\mu = 4{\cdot}90\) B.M.

(ii) Because CYANIDE is a STRONG field ligand and CHLORIDE a WEAK one, and only a strong field forces the electrons to pair.

Nickel is \(+2\) in both, so both start from \(3d^8\).

In \(\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}}\) cyanide forces those eight electrons into FOUR of the five d orbitals as four pairs. That frees ONE inner \(3d\) orbital, which with the \(4s\) and two \(4p\) gives \(dsp^2\) — SQUARE PLANAR — and with every electron paired the complex is DIAMAGNETIC.

In \(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}\) chloride cannot force any pairing, so the eight electrons spread out as far as Hund's rule allows, leaving TWO UNPAIRED and no \(3d\) orbital free. Bonding uses the \(4s\) and three \(4p\), giving \(sp^3\) — TETRAHEDRAL — and the complex is PARAMAGNETIC.

(iii) THREE ions. Only what sits outside the brackets ionises, and the two chlorido ligands INSIDE stay with the platinum:
\(\mathrm{[PtCl_2(NH_3)_4]Cl_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{[PtCl_2(NH_3)_4]^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{Cl^-}\)

The trap is the four chlorines in the formula: only the two outside the brackets are free.

rows.stem:
(i) Calculate the spin only magnetic moment of the complex \(\mathrm{[FeF_6]^{3-}}\). (Atomic number of Fe = 26)
(ii) Write the IUPAC name of the given complex :
\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Cl]Cl_2}\)
(iii) Why is the complex \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3+}}\) more stable than \(\mathrm{[CoF_6]^{3-}}\) ?
rows.solution:
(i) Iron is atomic number 26, and six fluorides give \(-6\) against an overall \(-3\), so iron is \(+3\) and \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) is \(3d^5\).

FLUORIDE is a WEAK field ligand and cannot force pairing, so all five electrons occupy separate orbitals — FIVE unpaired, the maximum any \(3d\) ion can have:
\(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{5 \times 7} = \sqrt{35}\)

\(\mu = 5{\cdot}92\ \mathrm{B.M.}\)

With cyanide, a strong field ligand, the same ion would pair four of them and the moment would fall to 1.73 B.M.

(ii) The five ammine ligands are neutral, the chlorido ligand gives \(-1\), and two chlorides sit outside — so cobalt must be \(+3\). Ligands are named in alphabetical order and the counter ion last:
PENTAAMMINECHLORIDOCOBALT(III) CHLORIDE

(iii) Because ethane-1,2-diamine is a CHELATING ligand and fluoride is not.

Ethane-1,2-diamine is BIDENTATE, binding the cobalt through both nitrogens at once and closing a five-membered ring; three of them close three rings. Fluoride is monodentate and closes none.

Two reasons make the chelate more stable: once one nitrogen has attached, the second is held close to the metal and binds readily; and releasing the ligand requires TWO bonds to break at once rather than one.

Ethane-1,2-diamine is also much the STRONGER field ligand of the two, so its individual bonds to the metal are stronger as well — both effects run the same way.

rows.stem:
Write the Nernst equation and calculate the emf of the following cell at 298 K :
\(\mathrm{Zn} \,|\, \mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\,(0{\cdot}001\ \mathrm{M}) \,\|\, \mathrm{H^{+}}\,(0{\cdot}01\ \mathrm{M}) \,|\, \mathrm{H_2}\,(\mathrm{g})\,(1\ \mathrm{bar}) \,|\, \mathrm{Pt}\,(\mathrm{s})\)
Given : \(\mathrm{E}^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}} = -\,0{\cdot}76\ \mathrm{V}\)
\(\mathrm{E}^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{H^{+}/H_2}} = 0{\cdot}00\ \mathrm{V}\)
[log 10 = 1]
rows.solution:
Read the cell diagram: zinc is on the LEFT and so is the anode, oxidised; hydrogen ions are reduced at the right.

\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}} = 0{\cdot}00 - (-0{\cdot}76) = 0{\cdot}76\ \mathrm{V}\)

The cell reaction is \(\mathrm{Zn} + 2\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} + \mathrm{H_2}\), so \(n = 2\). Solid zinc does not enter the quotient, and hydrogen at 1 bar contributes a factor of 1:
\(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{H^+}]^2}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}76 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{0{\cdot}001}{(0{\cdot}01)^2} = 0{\cdot}76 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{10^{-3}}{10^{-4}}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}76 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log 10 = 0{\cdot}76 - 0{\cdot}0295\)

\(E_{\text{cell}} = 0{\cdot}7305\ \mathrm{V}\)

The SQUARED term is where marks are lost: \((0{\cdot}01)^2\) is \(10^{-4}\), so the quotient is 10 and not \(10^{-1}\). The hydrogen ion's coefficient of 2 in the balanced equation carries through as an exponent in the Nernst quotient.
